title: Deuteron: compiler passes and innovations in three minutes

segments.title: The compiler transformations we built
segments.spoken: Deuteron compiles scheduled Emmy Kernel IR into PTX for the RTX 5090. Our contribution is guarded compiler passes that change memory reuse, parallel work, and tensor pipelines.
segments.brief_cue: Open on the presenter, then the title. Point to reuse, parallel work, and tensor pipelines.
segments.delivery: Start directly. Give the three transformation families one beat each.
segments.visual_cue: Show the title and the three contribution families: reuse data, redistribute work, and build tensor pipelines. Keep scheduled Emmy IR and RTX 5090 visible.

segments.title: Where our passes run
segments.spoken: We validate IR and metadata; each rewrite checks index and ownership conditions. Early passes vectorize loops, forward reduction inputs, reorder recurrences, and fold split-K grids. Specialized lowering follows; LLVM supplies optimization and NVPTX code generation.
segments.brief_cue: Follow the pipeline. Say the LLVM credit clearly.
segments.delivery: Follow the stages left to right. Read the early rewrite names as a sequence, not as separate claims of algorithmic invention.
segments.visual_cue: Show input validation, the actual early rewrite order, specialized lowering, and LLVM/NVPTX. The early order is vectorization, register forwarding, recurrence reordering, then grid folding. Name the project contribution: recognizers, guards, and transformed GPU schedules.

segments.title: Reuse data before loading it again
segments.spoken: We look for repeated reads of the same input, or neighboring values loaded one at a time. We keep reusable values in registers and load nearby values together. That means fewer repeated trips to global memory.
segments.brief_cue: Point to the repeated read, then show the saved values being reused.

segments.visual_cue: Show scalar loop to four values per lane; then load vector, reduce, and reuse the same vector in a consumer. Highlight matching indices, readonly input, closed lifetimes, and aligned complete coverage.

segments.title: Reshape parallel work
segments.spoken: We look for repeated calculations and blocks doing tiny pieces of work. We share dot products across threads, remove unnecessary reduction steps, and merge small pieces when enough parallel work remains. That reduces duplicated work and scheduling overhead.
segments.brief_cue: Show repeated work becoming shared work, then small pieces being combined.
segments.delivery: State the pattern first, then explain the change. Show repeated work becoming shared work, then small pieces being combined.
segments.visual_cue: Use two concrete illustrations: repeated dot to lane partials plus shuffle, and four eligible split-K partitions folded into two logical partitions with twice the K work. Label the factor-two drawing illustrative; the actual factor is guarded. Surplus physical CTAs exit; the original atomic output remains. The four partitions are per output tile within a larger grid; sufficient total parallelism remains a guard.

segments.title: Turn contractions into tensor work
segments.spoken: We look for matrix multiplication written as ordinary multiply-and-add loops. We replace them with tensor-core operations, using three lower-precision products to approximate the result while adding them together in 32-bit precision. We also arrange shared memory so tensor cores can read it efficiently.
segments.brief_cue: Follow the loop into tensor-core operations. Say that the result is approximate.

segments.title: Rewrite the pipeline feeding tensor cores
segments.spoken: We look for tensor-core loops that repeatedly copy and convert their matrix inputs. For the supported BF16 path, we fetch upcoming inputs early and pack them before the tensor cores need them. We also skip the final prefetch when there is no more work.
segments.brief_cue: Show the next inputs arriving early, then the unused final load being removed.

Keep the exact copy-phase guard visible. Show final unused prefetch/consumer barrier omitted while producer synchronization remains. TF32x3 and FP32 retain the eligible cp.async path.

segments.title: Recognize and stage the attention recurrence
segments.spoken: We look for attention loops that repeat the score calculation across output columns. We calculate scores once per group and reuse their weights. We also load neighboring keys together and reuse temporary storage once its values are no longer needed.
segments.brief_cue: Show one score calculation feeding several outputs, then temporary storage being reused.
segments.delivery: State the pattern first, then explain the change. Show one score calculation feeding several outputs, then temporary storage being reused.
segments.visual_cue: Show repeated score and online max/mass/value work becoming score reuse, row maximum, shared unnormalized weights, and separate mass/PV accumulation. Show two/four adjacent key rounds and read-to-maximum-to-store lifetime ordering in the same warp and component. Each unnormalized weight feeds register mass accumulation directly and shared storage for PV; mass does not reread shared weights.

segments.title: Redistribute probability–value work
segments.spoken: We look for attention loops where each thread scans every key for one output column. We split keys among thread groups, load four adjacent columns together, and combine their partial results. Each column keeps its original normalization.
segments.brief_cue: Show the keys split among groups, then their partial results being combined.

segments.title: Measure the whole compiler on RTX 5090
segments.spoken: On fifteen open workloads, geometric mean warm latency is three point seven five microseconds. Speedups are one point six six times over generated CUDA with NVCC, and one point one five times over the tested Triton baseline. All two hundred seventy calls passed the original checks. These are whole-compiler results with a limited Triton search.
